newsitem.title: USA: Eastman Chem sees supply/demand imbalance.
newsitem.headline: Eastman Chem sees supply/demand imbalance.

text.p: Eastman Chemical Co's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Earnest Deavenport, said he sees a significant supply/demand imbalance for Eastapak PET packaging plastic lasting through 1998.
He said demand for PET plastics continues to grow at double-digit rates, but capacity additions in 1997 and 1998 should be more than enough to meet that growth in demand.

Deavenport said that "worldwide increases in industry capacity, along with near-term additional capacity under construction, have created the conditions for the significant price erosion that has occurred for PET bottle resin."

"The lower prices do appear to be stimulating new applications, which will likely lead to greater demand," he said and "the prices, which are at less than reinvestment levels, now appear to have caused some in the industry to reconsider the desirability or the timing of additional capacity beyond that which is already under construction."

Deavenport concluded that "this should lead to a better balance and improving economics, but how long that will take depends on how fast demand grows. Our strategy assumes a significant imbalance lasting through 1998." The company expects PET industry capacity increases to keep PET prices under continued pressure.
Deavenport said both revenues and earnings were below first quarter 1996 levels, primarily as a result of lower prices for Eastapak PET.

Eastman reported net income of $72 million, or $0.92 per share, for the first quarter ended March 31, 1997, which was the same as the First Call consensus estimate, as compared with $112 million, or $1.39 per share, for 1996. The company said its sales declined seven percent to $1.17 billion for the quarter, down from $1.26 billion in 1996.
Eastman Chemical manufactures and markets chemicals, fibers and plastics.
